issues.legal_issue: An administrative authority conducting a revision that may affect civil rights must disclose adverse material on which it relies and give the affected parties a fair opportunity to respond.
material_facts: The State Government revised the demand for seigniorage fee after proceedings in which the Department relied on reports and inspection notes concerning the material excavated.
Those reports and inspection notes were not supplied to the affected contractors, and the revisional order did not refer to the inspection notes later relied on by the High Court.
The High Court rejected the objection that the material had not been disclosed, finding no demonstrated prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The revisional process disregarded natural justice. The High Court order was set aside, and the matter was remitted for reconsideration after the reports and inspection notes relied on by the Department were supplied to the contractors.
issues.legal_principle: The audi alteram partem rule requires fair notice of the case to be met and an adequate opportunity to respond before an adverse order affecting civil consequences is made. Natural justice applies to administrative as well as quasi-judicial action. The Court relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works, Board of Education v. Rice, and Spackman v. Plumstead District Board of Works.

predicates.administrative_revision_affecting_civil_: An administrative authority conducts a revision that may affect a person's civil rights or interests.
predicates.authority_relied_on_adverse_material: The authority relies on material that may support an adverse decision against an affected person.
predicates.affected_party_was_not_given_that_materi: The affected person was not given the material on which the authority relied.

issues.definition: When an authority conducting a revision affecting civil rights relies on adverse material that it has not disclosed to the affected person, the adverse order requires reconsideration after disclosure.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing authority must consider the effect of a department's earlier admission on a material fact when reconsidering the dispute.
material_facts: In earlier proceedings, the Department had admitted that the contractors used earth as filling material.
The Department later explained that the earlier statement was a mistake and that it had lacked precise knowledge of the excavation locations and the nature of the soil.
The High Court accepted that explanation without adequately addressing the earlier admission.
The Supreme Court directed the State Government on remand to consider the effect of the Department's earlier concession.
issues.conclusion: On reconsideration, the State Government must consider the effect of the Department's concession in the earlier proceedings; the Supreme Court did not finally determine what weight or binding effect the concession has.
issues.legal_principle: A material admission in earlier proceedings must be taken into account when the dispute is reconsidered. The Court relied on the record of the earlier proceedings and expressly directed the State Government to consider the concession's effect.

predicates.administrative_reconsideration_of_a_disp: An administrative authority is reconsidering a dispute after a reviewing court has remitted it.
predicates.department_made_prior_admission_on_mater: The department previously made an admission about a fact material to the dispute.

issues.definition: When an administrative authority reconsiders a remitted dispute and the department previously admitted a material fact, the authority must consider the effect of that admission.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of administrative discretion does not permit a court to substitute its view for the authority's, but permits intervention where the action is so unfair or unreasonable that no reasonable authority would have taken it.
material_facts: The State Government exercised revisional authority in a dispute concerning demands for seigniorage fee.
The High Court assessed the Government's decision and the material before it, including inspection notes not referred to in the revisional order.
The Supreme Court held that judicial review is not an appeal on the merits and that the High Court's conclusions about the undisclosed material and absence of prejudice were unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: A court reviewing administrative action may not substitute its judgment for the authority's; it may intervene when the action is so unfair or unreasonable that no reasonable authority would have taken it. The High Court's assessment in this case was unsustainable in light of the natural-justice defects.
issues.legal_principle: Administrative discretion may involve a choice between reasonable courses of action, and judicial review is not an appeal on law or fact. Intervention is justified where the authority acts unreasonably in the relevant sense, including by failing to consider required matters or considering irrelevant ones. The Court relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, Secretary of State for Education and Science v. Metropolitan Borough Council of Tameside, and Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation.

predicates.judicial_review_of_administrative_discre: A court is reviewing an administrative authority's exercise of discretion.
predicates.administrative_action_is_so_unfair_or_un: The administrative action is so unfair or unreasonable that no reasonable authority would have taken it.

issues.definition: A court reviewing administrative discretion may intervene when the action is so unfair or unreasonable that no reasonable authority would have taken it.
